content: The study focuses on ophthalmological evaluations related to ocular infections caused by microfilariae in the anterior segment of the eye. It is a prospective observational study that identified one serious case and one non-serious case, with confirmation in 12 instances and non-confirmation in 11. The study highlights that the population and focus may not be representative of other regions due to variations in resources and accessibility. After 12–16 years of mass drug administration (MDA) and 32–35 years post-MDA cessation, microfilarial prevalence was found to be below 1% in 90% of sampled villages and below 5% in 100% of villages. In two out of three foci, transmission interruption was confirmed, with no positive cases in children based on Ov-16 serology (0%, 95% CI: 0–0.1%) and no ocular morbidity (0%, 95% CI: 0–0.8%). The diagnostic accuracy of O-150 PCR testing of skin snips was compared to skin snip microscopy. Sensitivity ranged from 71% to 100%, while specificity ranged from 15% to 100%. However, pooling results was not feasible due to heterogeneity and high risk of bias. The O-150 PCR test performed better in low-prevalence settings, with unpublished data suggesting improved sensitivity compared to microscopy. Sensitivity ranged from 81% to 98%, and specificity ranged from 89% to 100%. However, pooling results was again not possible due to heterogeneity and high risk of bias. For vector surveillance, O-150 PCR pool screening in black flies was compared to traditional dissection methods. No significant differences were found between the two methods, and newer DNA extraction techniques with larger pool sizes showed similar performance to traditional methods. While O-150 PCR has higher initial costs, it reduces long-term expenses, especially with increased pool sizes. The study emphasizes the challenges of diagnostic testing in low-prevalence settings, the limitations of skin snip microscopy as a reference standard, and the need for reliable tools to confirm the interruption of transmission and elimination of onchocerciasis.
